lesson.body:
Here's the surprise that explains almost everything: squeeze nearly any wine grape, dark or pale, and the juice runs basically clear. Colour lives in the skins, like dye in a teabag. So the real difference between red, white and rosé isn't the grape, it's how long that juice steeps with the skins.

Red wine ferments right alongside the crushed skins for days or weeks, soaking up deep colour plus tannin, the grippy, slightly drying feeling on your gums (think strong black tea or biting an unripe banana). White wine usually presses the skins away first, so the pale juice ferments largely on its own. Rosé sits in between, with the juice kissing the skins for just a few hours, long enough to blush pink but not turn red. (Skin-contact "orange" whites prove the point: leave white juice on its skins and it turns deep and tannic too.)

One last myth-buster: because colour lives in the skins, dark grapes can make wine of almost any colour, depending on the winemaker's timing. Light grapes are the exception, with no colour to give, they essentially only make white.
outcomes: Explain why nearly all grape juice runs clear
Describe how skin time shapes red, white and rosé
Recognise tannin as the grippy feeling from skins

deep_notes: The colour comes from pigments called anthocyanins, stored in the skin. The same family of pigments colours blueberries and red cabbage. Educators say 'nearly' any grape because of a small group called teinturiers, French for dyers, whose flesh is red too. Alicante Bouschet is the best-known example, and growers have long planted it to deepen the colour of paler red blends.

Skin thickness shapes a red wine. Thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon gives deep colour and firm tannin, while thin-skinned Pinot Noir makes paler, silkier wines. Tannin also comes from the pips, the seeds inside the grape. You feel it as dryness because tannin binds to proteins in your saliva, the ones that normally keep your mouth slippery. The time the juice spends soaking on the skins has a name: maceration.

Besides a few hours on the skins, there are two other common routes to rosé. Direct pressing squeezes dark grapes gently, so the juice picks up only a faint blush, which gives very pale styles such as many Provence rosés. Saignée, French for 'bleeding', draws off some juice early from a tank that is on its way to becoming red. In the EU, rosé generally cannot be made by mixing red and white wine, but rosé Champagne is a famous exception.

Champagne shows this best. Most of the grapes grown there are dark, Pinot Noir and Meunier, yet most Champagne is white. The grapes are pressed gently, often as whole bunches, so the skins give up as little colour as possible. A Champagne made only from dark grapes is labelled blanc de noirs, 'white from blacks'. One made only from light grapes, usually Chardonnay, is blanc de blancs.

deeper.body: Skin-contact whites are nothing new. Georgia has made wine for about 8,000 years, and many producers there still ferment light grapes with their skins in qvevri: large clay jars buried in the ground. The skins can stay in for months. The result is amber in colour, with some tannin and notes of dried apricot, tea and nuts.
deeper.title: Georgia's ancient amber wines

deeper.q: What makes a traditional Georgian amber wine amber?
deeper.why: The colour, and the tannin, come from the skins of light grapes left in the clay jar for a long soak.

deeper.body: Some grapes are neither properly dark nor light. Pinot Grigio, called Pinot Gris in France, has greyish-pink skins. Pressed quickly, it makes a white wine. Left on its skins for a short time, from several hours to a few days, the wine turns a pale copper. In north-east Italy this style is called ramato, the Italian word for coppery.
deeper.title: Grey grapes, copper wine

deeper.q: A copper-tinted Pinot Grigio has had some red wine added to it.
deeper.why: The copper tint comes from the grape's own greyish-pink skins during a short soak. Nothing is added.

deeper.body: A young red is often purple at the rim. Over the years, its colour pigments slowly bind with tannin, and some drop out as sediment, so the wine fades towards garnet, then brick or tawny. Whites go the other way. They deepen from pale lemon to gold, and eventually to amber.
deeper.title: Colour keeps changing in the bottle

A white that has turned golden
A red with a bright purple rim
A white that is pale lemon-green
deeper.q: Which of these are signs of an older wine?
deeper.why: Reds fade towards brick as they age, while whites deepen towards gold. Purple reds and pale lemon-green whites are usually young.

v2.body:
In 2004 a British wine merchant, **David A. Harvey**, needed a name for white wines fermented on their skins, like reds, which came out amber and a little drying on the gums. He called them **orange wine**, after the colour, not the fruit, and the name stuck. The style is ancient; the name shows the rule behind this lesson.

Nearly any wine grape's juice runs almost clear. The colour sits in the skins, like tea in a teabag. Skin time also brings **tannin**, the slightly drying feel on your gums (think strong black tea or an unripe banana). Red wine ferments with its skins for days or weeks. White is usually pressed off them first. Rosé gets a few hours, usually about 2 to 20.

So one dark grape can land anywhere on a dial. Press it gently at once and you get a white, **blanc de noirs**. Let the juice catch a faint tint as it is pressed and you get **vin gris** (gris is French for grey), the palest pink: Lorraine's Côtes de Toul makes it mainly from Gamay and Pinot Noir. Next come rosé, then **clairet**, Bordeaux's deep pink or light red, left on the skins for roughly one to two days: the wine behind the English word claret, used for red Bordeaux. White grapes have no red to give: they essentially make only white wine, or amber orange wine after a long soak.

Rosé itself has three routes:
• Direct pressing: dark grapes pressed straight away, for the palest pinks such as vin gris.
• Short soak: crushed grapes rest on their skins for hours, then are pressed.
• **Saignée** (French for bleeding): pink juice drawn off a tank that is becoming red, which leaves the red more concentrated.
Mixing red and white wine is not a route: EU rules forbid it for still rosé, and rosé Champagne is the famous exception.

Soaking pulls things out of the skins, and it happens in order. Colour comes first: it peaks within the first few days of a red's soak, then can even fade a little. Tannin keeps building for longer, and tannin from the seeds needs time and alcohol. The skins hold many aroma compounds too.

Four things speed this up: warmth, alcohol (it helps dissolve tannin), contact (pushing the floating skins back into the juice) and crushing, which breaks the skins open.

Side by side, rosé and orange wine pull the two jobs apart. White skins hold almost no red colour, so days, weeks or even months on them give amber colour and real tannin. Dark skins for a few hours give colour with little tannin.
deep_notes: The style is far older than the name: Georgia has made amber wines in clay jars for thousands of years. In Europe it came back through Friuli, in north-east Italy, where Josko Gravner turned to long skin contact in the late 1990s. He, like many Georgians, prefers the word amber. The Oxford Companion to Wine puts the skin contact for these wines at anywhere from about a week to a year.

Where a wine lands on the dial depends on the grape as well as the clock. Thick, dark skins such as Cabernet Sauvignon's give colour fast, while thin-skinned Pinot Noir stays paler even after a long soak. The pigments are anthocyanins, the same family that colours blueberries. A few teinturier grapes, such as Alicante Bouschet, have red flesh as well, so even their juice is coloured and they cannot make a white.

Côtes de Toul, near Nancy in Lorraine, makes three colours: white, red and gris. Champagne uses the same gentle, immediate pressing on its dark grapes, but there the aim is no colour at all: that is blanc de noirs. In both places the press is worked softly, because squeezing hard pushes more colour and tannin out of the skins.

Clairet is a traditional term within the Bordeaux appellation (the region's legally protected name), made from its usual dark grapes, mostly Merlot and the two Cabernets. It shares its name with the medieval pale red behind the word claret, though today's clairet is a small, deliberate style, darker than rosé. Some producers present it as a deep rosé, others as a pale red: it sits right on the border.

Scientists who track a red's soak see the same curve again and again. Colour rises fast and peaks after about four or five days, then dips a little, as some pigment clings back onto skins and yeast or joins other compounds. Tannin from the skins comes early too, but tannin from the seeds needs a longer soak, and it dissolves more easily once alcohol has formed.

White grape skins are not empty: they hold tannin and yellow pigments, just almost none of the red ones. A long soak draws these out, and contact with air during the long process can deepen the colour towards amber, the way a cut apple browns. That is why orange wines run from deep gold to copper and tea brown. A short soak on greyish-pink skins gives the copper ramato Pinot Grigio of north-east Italy.

deeper.body: Red colour in a grape skin is switched on by a pair of neighbouring genes. In white grapes both are broken; in one of them, a stretch of so-called jumping DNA silences it. Studies suggest this white form arose only once or a few times, and almost every white variety inherited it. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations of Pinot Noir.
deeper.title: White grapes are dark grapes with switches off

deeper.key: In white grapes the genes that switch on red colour in the skin are broken.
opts: Its red colour genes are off
Its juice holds too much acid
Its seeds soak up the colour
deeper.q: Why can a white grape never make a red wine, however long it soaks?
deeper.remember: White grapes: the red switch is off.
deeper.why: With no red colour in the skins, skin time can only give gold or amber.

deeper.body: Still rosé may not be a blend of red and white wine, but Germany has a pale red that comes close. A Rotling is made by mixing red and white grapes, or their crushed mash, before fermentation, never by blending finished wines. Württemberg's version is Schillerwein, often Trollinger with Riesling; the name comes from schillern, to shimmer. It may not be labelled rosé.
deeper.title: Germany mixes the grapes, not the wines

deeper.key: Schillerwein is a Rotling: red and white grapes, or their mash, mixed before fermentation.
deeper.q: A Schillerwein is made by blending finished red and white wines.
deeper.why: Mixing finished wines is not allowed, so the colour still comes from skins during pressing and fermentation.

deeper.body: Some cellars heat crushed red grapes to about 70°C, for minutes up to an hour or so, before fermentation. This is thermovinification. Heat breaks the skin cells open, so colour floods out fast. That colour can be less stable unless enough tannin joins it, so the method suits soft, fruity reds made to drink young. It also rescues colour in grapes touched by rot.
deeper.title: Heat can pull colour out in hours

deeper.key: Thermovinification heats crushed red grapes so colour floods out fast.
deeper.q: What does heating crushed red grapes mainly speed up?
deeper.remember: Heat first: colour fast, made to drink young.
deeper.why: Without enough tannin that colour can be less stable, so it suits soft reds made to drink young.
